about: The prayer Leo XIII composed and ordered to be said after low Mass; among his prayers it stands after the Salve Regína and the collect. Three petitions and three different postures: first a plea to Michael for defence, then a wish that God command the enemy, and last a charge to Michael again, this time a long one, with a whole train of objects before the verb. The name Míchaël is Hebrew for “who is like God”, and the prayer says exactly that when it leaves the commanding to God and the carrying out to the Archangel.

s01.translation: Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in battle. Be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil.

s02.translation: May God rebuke him, we humbly pray.

s03.translation: And do thou, O Prince of the heavenly hosts, by the power of God, thrust into hell Satan, and all the evil spirits, who prowl about the world seeking the ruin of souls. Amen.

w011.function: The noun exists only in the plural — in Latin an ambush is always ambushes.

w013.function: The future imperative — the form Latin uses for orders meant to hold from now on, not only at this moment. The plain imperative would be “es”.

w015.function: Subjunctive of wish, and not a request to Michael: the commanding is God's. The verb governs the dative — hence “illi” (w016), not an accusative. The received English says “rebuke”, after the Greek of Jude 9; the Latin imperet is command.

w018.function: An adjective in the nominative plural — “we, suppliant, pray” — rendered adverbially, as English wants it.

w019.function: A deponent: passive in form, active in meaning.

w020.function: The pronoun is spoken, though Latin usually leaves it out — because the sentence turns here from God back to Michael. The conjunction -que is hung on the end of it.

w023.function: Genitive: it agrees with “milítiæ” (w022), not with “Princeps” (w021). The host is heavenly, not its captain.

w025.function: It declines like a pronoun: genitive “alíus”, dative “álii”, not like the -us, -a, -um adjectives. The -que hung on it joins it to “sátanam” (w024).

w032.function: A deponent; the compound of per and vagor means to wander the whole length and breadth of a place.

w036.function: Ablative of means: Michael casts them down not by his own strength but by God's.

w039.function: The verb comes last of all, after every object: Latin holds the command back to the final word.
